Equivalent sets
Two finite sets A and B are said to be equivalent, if n(A) = n(B). Clearly, equal sets are equivalent
but equivalent sets need not be equal.
Example
The sets A = {4, 5, 3, 2} and B = {1, 6, 8, 9} are equivalent but are not equal.
Subset
Let A and B be two sets. If every element of A is an element of B, then A is called a subset of B
and we write A ⊂ B or B ⊃ A (read as “ A is contained in B” or “ B contains A”). B is called the
superset of A.
Note
• Every set is a subset and a superset of itself.
• If A is not a subset of B, we write A ̸⊂ B.
• The empty set is the subset of every set.
• If A is a set with n(A) = m, then the number of subsets of A is 2m and the number of
proper subsets of A is 2m − 1.
Example
Let A = {3, 4}, then the subsets of A are ϕ, {3}, {4}, {3, 4}.
Here, n(A) = 2 and number of subsets of A = 2 2 = 4.
